newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean banks cooperate to avoid bankruptcies.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean banks cooperate to avoid bankruptcies.

text.p: Financial institutions have agreed to set up a committee to help finance companies short of cash, the Korea Federation of Banks said on Tuesday.
The committee, which will include local banks, merchant banking corporations, securities houses and life insurers, will screen financially troubled firms and decide which will receive assistance.
"We decided to take joint action because it is difficult for a major lender, acting alone, to aid seriously troubled companies," said federation vice-chairman Kim Jong-sung.

Earlier on Tuesday, the presidents of several domestic banks met to discuss the plan to provide assistance. Senior officials at the banks agreed in principle to launch the committee through which they will decide to support a financially troubled company or let it go bankrupt, a federation official said.
The federation's move came the day after the country's 19th-biggest business conglomerate, the Jinro Group, said it would sell some business lines and assets because of financial pressures.
"Creditors are expected to help finance Jinro, given its impact on the economy and in the financial industry," said Lee In-hyung, research director of LG Economic Research Institute.
The Commercial Bank of Korea, Jinro's primary creditor, said it would consider fresh loans to the group if the conglomerate presented an acceptable restructuring plan.

The committee, which will begin work next Monday, will assist troubled companies as long they are not facing imminent bankruptcy. One goal of the committee is to become involved with a company before serious problems and market rumours surface, a federation statement said.

Korean financial institutions, non-banking financial institutions, have been reluctant of late to extend fresh loans to companies rumoured to be experiencing serious cash shortages. This has led to an increase in debt defaults among smaller firms and rising non-performing loans in the financial industry.

The financial industry was hit hard by this year's collapse of the flagship affiliates of two big conglomerates, the Hanbo Group, which is at the centre of a growing national corruption scandal, and the Sammi Group.
"The move is aimed at preventing what has become a vicious circle," said Lee Hwa-yeol, banking analyst at Ssangyong Securities. "And this reflects how great the impact of Sammi and Hanbo has been."
Analysts said formation of the committee might provide a short-term psychological boost to the economy and the stock market. But they added that meaningful results were unlikely.
Financial shares were hardly moved on the news. The financial-sub index rose 3.47 points to 518.75 on Tuesday.
"It will help stabilise the financial industry from a psychological point of view. It's very symbolic," said LG's Lee. "But I question if the 'gentlemen's agreement' has a real binding force."
Rhee Namuh, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine, said "inefficient allocation of capital" had caused problems in Korean financial institutions.
"The collective action will not help resolve their problems," Rhee said. "A bank should take the risk responsibility for a loan based on its credit analysis."
Analysts said Jinro's bid to generate more cash by selling assets, including property, would likely fall short as the company would probably have trouble getting the price it wanted.
South Korea has experienced asset deflation on falling property prices.
